cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Always write answers in the context of the question: if the data is about rainfall, say ‘rainfall’ not ‘the data’ or ‘the values’

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Support every statement with a specific data value: ‘The median rainfall in July (68 mm) was higher than in April (42 mm)’

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Avoid vague language: replace ‘quite high’, ‘bigger’, ‘a lot’ with precise values and comparisons

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: When comparing distributions, always compare both location (median/mean) AND spread (IQR/range/SD)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Use comparative conjunctions: ‘higher than’, ‘lower than’, ‘more spread than’, ‘less variable than’

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: When describing a graph or chart, comment on: overall pattern, key features (peaks, troughs), any anomalies, and the shape of the distribution

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: In a conclusion, state whether the hypothesis is supported, quote supporting data, and note any limitations

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: When communicating to a non-specialist audience, avoid technical jargon or explain it; use everyday language with statistics to back up claims

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: A good statistical sentence has three parts: observation + evidence + context (e.g. ‘On average, girls scored higher (median 72 vs 65), which may reflect greater engagement with homework’)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: When writing about correlation, state the direction and strength, then distinguish correlation from causation

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Use connective words to structure answers: ‘however’, ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’, ‘furthermore’ for coherent arguments

cards.front: Recall a key point about Statistical Writing Communication
cards.back: Never just describe a visual pattern without quoting numbers: ‘the bar is higher’ earns no marks; ‘the bar for London (3.2 million) is roughly double that for Bristol (1.6 million)’ does

cards.front: What should you know about gcse statistics exam tips — statistical writing & communication?
cards.back: 1. For Statistical Writing & Communication questions, show every step of your working clearly — method marks count even if the final answer is wrong 2. Check your answer makes sense in context (estimation, units, reasonableness) 3. Use correct mathematical notation and state formulae before substituting values 4. If a Statistical Writing & Communication question asks you to 'prove' or 'show', write a logical chain of reasoning with a conclusion line 5. For problem-solving, identify the topic first, then recall the relevant method
A study compares weekly screen time for two age groups. 11–14 year olds: median 21 hours, IQR 10 hours. 15–18 year olds: median 28 hours, IQR 14 hours. Write a comparison.
